regiones/egipto/resumen.texto: Civilization of the Nile valley and delta, with a written history of more than four thousand years. Its texts, monuments and papyri, preserved by the dry climate, are one of the greatest firsthand sources on Antiquity. It later became a Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Islamic and Ottoman province.

regiones/egipto/eras.0.resumen.texto: Neolithic and Chalcolithic cultures of the valley (Badarian, Naqada) with growing social hierarchy, leading to regional kingdoms and unification.

regiones/egipto/eras.1.resumen.texto: First kings of a unified Egypt, with their capital at Memphis and royal necropolises at Abydos. The dates of this and the following periods are conventional and may vary by decades depending on the author.

regiones/egipto/eras.2.resumen.texto: Age of the great pyramids, from Djoser at Saqqara to Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure at Giza, with a centralized state and an administration of viziers and scribes.

regiones/egipto/eras.3.resumen.texto: Fragmentation of central power, with rival dynasties at Herakleopolis and Thebes, until reunification by Mentuhotep II.

regiones/egipto/eras.4.resumen.texto: Theban reunification and the height of the 12th Dynasty, with its capital at Itjtawy; classical age of Egyptian literature and expansion into Nubia.

regiones/egipto/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Hyksos, of Asiatic origin, rule the delta from Avaris, while a Theban dynasty resists until their expulsion by Ahmose I.

regiones/egipto/eras.6.resumen.texto: Egypt as an imperial power in Nubia and the Levant: Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II. It ends with the fragmentation of the state.

regiones/egipto/eras.7.resumen.texto: Kings at Tanis, high priests of Amun at Thebes, Libyan dynasties and the Kushite dynasty (XXV), which rules Egypt until the Assyrian invasion.

regiones/egipto/eras.8.resumen.texto: Saite revival (26th Dynasty), Achaemenid Persian rule, the last native dynasty (XXX) and Persian reconquest before Alexander.

regiones/egipto/eras.9.resumen.texto: After Alexander's conquest, the Ptolemies rule from Alexandria and combine Egyptian and Greek traditions; it ends with Cleopatra VII.

regiones/egipto/eras.10.resumen.texto: Imperial province under an equestrian governor and granary of Rome; Alexandria is one of the great cities of the Mediterranean.

regiones/egipto/eras.11.resumen.texto: Province of the Eastern Roman Empire with the rise of Christianity, monasticism and Christological disputes; brief Sasanian occupation (619-629).

regiones/egipto/eras.12.resumen.texto: Arab conquest and rule by caliphs and governors (Rashidun, Umayyads, Abbasids, then Tulunids and Ikhshidids), with Fustat as capital and gradual Arabization.

regiones/egipto/eras.13.resumen.texto: The Fatimids found Cairo and the mosque-university of al-Azhar; Egypt is the center of an Ismaili caliphate.

regiones/egipto/eras.14.resumen.texto: Saladin overthrows the Fatimids and restores Sunnism; Egypt is the base of the struggle against the crusaders.

regiones/egipto/eras.15.resumen.texto: A military elite of slave origin rules Egypt and Syria from Cairo and defeats the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260).

regiones/egipto/eras.16.resumen.texto: Province of the Ottoman Empire after the conquest by Selim I, with real power often in the hands of Mamluk beys; French occupation from 1798 to 1801.

regiones/egipto/eras.17.resumen.texto: Muhammad Ali and his successors modernize the country; the Suez Canal opens (1869) and Britain occupies Egypt from 1882. It ends with the 1952 revolution.

regiones/egipto/eras.18.resumen.texto: The Free Officers overthrow the monarchy in 1952; Naguib is the first president (1953–1954) and Nasser succeeds him. Nasser nationalizes the Suez Canal (1956), Egypt joins Syria in the United Arab Republic (1958–1961), and the defeat of 1967 precedes his death in 1970.

regiones/egipto/eras.19.resumen.texto: After the 1973 war, Sadat opens the economy and signs the Camp David Accords (1978) and peace with Israel (1979); he is assassinated in 1981.

regiones/egipto/eras.20.resumen.texto: Almost thirty years of rule under a near-permanent state of emergency, with economic reforms and strong Islamist opposition; it ends with the protests of 2011.

regiones/egipto/demografia.7.nota.texto: Around the time of unification. Bruce Trigger proposes about 2 million.

regiones/egipto/demografia.9.nota.texto: Middle Kingdom, with more cultivation in the Fayum and the Delta.

regiones/egipto/demografia.10.nota.texto: Ramesside period. Using the ratio of urban to total population (1 to 7), Butzer himself arrives at 3 to 3.5 million; Barry Kemp proposes 4 to 5 million.

regiones/egipto/demografia.11.nota.texto: Ptolemaic period. Figures based on the poll tax and on classical authors give more, up to about 7.5 million.

regiones/egipto/demografia.12.nota.texto: Diodorus states that the population had reached 7 million in ancient times and that in his day it was no less than 3 million.

regiones/egipto/demografia.14.nota.texto: Josephus gives it excluding Alexandria; modern historians consider it excessive.

regiones/egipto/religiones.2.nombre.texto: Judaism (community of Alexandria and other cities)

regiones/egipto/religiones.0.nota.texto: With syncretic Greco-Roman cults (Serapis, Isis) from the Ptolemaic period; the decline accelerates after the edict of Theodosius of 391.

regiones/egipto/religiones.2.nota.texto: Large diaspora, hit hard after the revolt of 115-117.

regiones/egipto/religiones.3.nota.texto: Highly uncertain estimate: there are no religious censuses; conversion is reconstructed from names in papyri (Bagnall, 1993, Egypt in Late Antiquity).

regiones/egipto/religiones.4.nota.texto: Approximate majority from the 4th century; after 451 the Coptic Church breaks with Chalcedon. The timeline of conversion to Islam is debated.

regiones/egipto/religiones.6.nota.texto: It was the religion of the dynasty and its court; the Muslim population remained mostly Sunni.

regiones/egipto/religiones.7.nota.texto: The Muslim majority is placed between the 10th and 14th centuries depending on the author; the exact pace is uncertain.

regiones/egipto/idiomas.4.nota.texto: It declines as a spoken language in favor of Arabic; it survives as a liturgical language.

regiones/bajo-egipto/resumen.texto: The Nile delta and the region from Memphis northward, with cities such as Memphis, Heliopolis, Avaris, Pi-Ramesses and, later, Alexandria. The Egyptians conceived of it as one of the two lands unified by the king.

regiones/alto-egipto/resumen.texto: The narrow Nile valley between Memphis and the First Cataract (Aswan), with Abydos, Thebes and Elephantine. It was the cradle of several ruling houses and the setting of the great necropolises of the New Kingdom.

regiones/nubia/resumen.texto: The Nile valley south of the First Cataract, today divided between Egypt and Sudan. Home to the kingdoms of Kerma, Kush and Napata-Meroë, it supplied gold and mercenaries to Egypt and, in the 25th Dynasty, ruled it.

regiones/nubia/eras.2.nombre.texto: Nubia under the Egyptian New Kingdom

regiones/nubia/eras.6.nombre.texto: Christian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia

regiones/nubia/eras.7.nombre.texto: Sultanate of Sennar and Ottoman Nubia

regiones/nubia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Group A, the first powerful society of Lower Nubia, reached its height around 3100 BC and disappeared around 2900 BC; in the south, Pre-Kerma preceded Kerma.

regiones/nubia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Kerma, which dominated the valley between the first and fourth cataracts, came to rival Egypt around 1750–1500 BC; in Lower Nubia lived Group C (around 2400–1550 BC).

regiones/nubia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Egypt absorbed Kerma around 1500 BC and governed Nubia with a viceroy of Kush, fortresses and temples; rebellions continued for centuries.

regiones/nubia/eras.3.resumen.texto: After the Egyptian collapse, Kush reorganized at Napata; Kashta and Piye founded the 25th Dynasty (8th century BC), which ruled Egypt until the Assyrian invasion in the mid-7th century BC.

regiones/nubia/eras.4.resumen.texto: The capital moved to Meroë and the kingdom, which the Greeks called Ethiopia, became more African in art and language; it declined in the 4th century with the Noba, the Blemmyes and the invasion of Axum.

regiones/nubia/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Noba, who brought the Nubian languages, and the Blemmyes divided the valley; from the fall of Kush emerged Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia.

regiones/nubia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Nobatia converted in 543, Makuria in the mid-6th century and Alodia in 580; the Treaty of Baqt (652) ensured centuries of peace with Egypt. Makuria absorbed Nobatia and declined from the 13th century because of the Mamluks and other factors; around 1500 Soba fell.

regiones/nubia/eras.7.resumen.texto: The Funj of Sennar (1504) spread from the third cataract southward and promoted Islam and Arabization; the Ottomans occupied Lower Nubia in the 1560s. The Turco-Egyptian conquest (1820–1821) ended both.

regiones/nubia/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Traditional Nubian religion (Group A, Kerma and Group C)

regiones/nubia/religiones.2.nombre.texto: Kushite religion: Amun of Jebel Barkal and Nubian gods

regiones/nubia/religiones.6.nombre.texto: Traditional religions and the cult of Isis at Philae

regiones/nubia/religiones.0.nota.texto: No texts: it is known from the tombs of Kerma, which were very rich, with burials of companions and animals, and from the imagery of lions and other animals.

regiones/nubia/religiones.1.nota.texto: Temples and the cult of Amun of the Egyptian administration; how much of it the Nubian population adopted is unclear.

regiones/nubia/religiones.2.nota.texto: The kings of Kush venerate Amun of Jebel Barkal and Nubian gods; their roots lie in the animist Kerma culture, with lions and other animals (Kushite religion).

regiones/nubia/religiones.3.nota.texto: The kings of Kush venerate Amun of Jebel Barkal in Egyptian forms, and Egyptian and Nubian gods merge.

regiones/nubia/religiones.4.nota.texto: Indigenous practices continued despite Egyptian colonization and religious fusion.

regiones/nubia/religiones.5.nota.texto: With Meroë, Nubian gods gain weight, such as the lion Apedemak, though Amun and Isis remain.

regiones/nubia/religiones.6.nota.texto: Sources are scarce. The Noba and Blemmyes venerated Isis at Philae until Justinian closed the temple, around 535–537.

regiones/nubia/religiones.7.nota.texto: Nobatia (543), Makuria (mid-6th century) and Alodia (580) converted. Nobatia and Alodia were Miaphysite according to John of Ephesus; Makuria was Chalcedonian, and its later ties with the Coptic Church are disputed.

regiones/nubia/religiones.8.nota.texto: After the Mamluks and the Arab tribes, Makuria had Muslim kings in 1310–1320; the Islamization of the population was gradual.

regiones/nubia/religiones.9.nota.texto: The Funj attracted Sufis and favored Islam; Christianity faded.

regiones/nubia/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Ancient Nubia (Group A, Pre-Kerma, Kerma, Group C)

regiones/nubia/culturas.7.nombre.texto: Nubia under the Funj and the Ottomans

regiones/nubia/culturas.0.nota.texto: The names are modern archaeological labels: it is not known what the people called themselves. Kerma was a melting pot with Saharan, Central African and Levantine roots.

regiones/nubia/culturas.2.nota.texto: Officials, soldiers and priests in the fortresses and temples.

regiones/nubia/culturas.3.nota.texto: With many Egyptian affinities, but distinct from Egypt in culture, language and ethnicity, as Egyptian art distinguished it.

regiones/nubia/culturas.4.nota.texto: The Noba gave their name to Nubia; the Blemmyes dominated the north. Sources are scarce.

regiones/nubia/culturas.5.nota.texto: Literature in Nubian, Greek and Coptic.

regiones/nubia/culturas.6.nota.texto: Migration of Arab tribes into the Nile valley from the 14th century, and an Arabization that accelerated with the Funj.

regiones/nubia/culturas.7.nota.texto: The Funj, of uncertain ethnic origin and Arabized, governed a diverse population of Nubians, Beja, Bedouins and Hamaj.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.0.nombre.texto: Languages of Pre-Kerma, Kerma and Group C

regiones/nubia/idiomas.6.nombre.texto: Nubian languages (Old Nubian from the 8th century)

regiones/nubia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: The language of Kerma has no texts. According to Claude Rilly it was probably already Meroitic (there are Meroitic names in the Egyptian execration texts of the 12th Dynasty about Kerma); others propose a Cushitic or Nilo-Saharan language.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: The language of officials and inscriptions; it need not have been that of the population.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: According to Claude Rilly (Meroitic language), there are Meroitic names and words in Egyptian texts of the Napatan period, and already in the 12th Dynasty execration texts about Kerma; the language was not yet written down.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: The kings of Kush used Egyptian hieroglyphs until Meroitic writing appeared.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.4.nota.texto: Written since around the 2nd century BC; the script can be read, but the language is little understood.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.5.nota.texto: The Blemmyes are usually identified with the ancestors of the Beja.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Introduced by the Noba after the fall of Kush; Old Nubian was written from the 8th to the 15th century.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.7.nota.texto: Written language alongside Nubian and Coptic; in Makuria there are inscriptions in Greek until the 12th century.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.8.nota.texto: Written language of the Church, alongside Nubian and Greek.

regiones/nubia/idiomas.9.nota.texto: It spread with the Arab tribes and with Islam; its weight varies greatly from area to area.

fuentes/paleta-de-narmer/resumen.texto: Ceremonial palette found at Hierakonpolis, showing King Narmer wearing the White Crown and the Red Crown. It is one of the earliest depictions of royal power and of hieroglyphic signs.

fuentes/paleta-de-narmer/por_que_importa.texto: It is often read as an image of the country's unification, although that meaning is debated.

fuentes/piedra-de-palermo/resumen.texto: Fragment of royal annals from the 5th Dynasty that lists kings and events year by year, including predynastic kings. Its exact provenance is unknown.

fuentes/piedra-de-palermo/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the few Egyptian sources that reconstruct the earliest king list and the Nile floods.

fuentes/piedra-de-palermo/leer.0.titulo.texto: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 1 (1906), Internet Archive

fuentes/textos-de-las-piramides/resumen.texto: Body of spells and hymns carved in the chambers of pyramids of the 5th and 6th Dynasties, the oldest surviving religious corpus of Egypt. They ensure the king's resurrection and his ascent to the sky.

fuentes/textos-de-las-piramides/por_que_.texto: They show the funerary beliefs of the Old Kingdom and solar and Osirian theology in its earliest form.

fuentes/textos-de-las-piramides/leer.0.t.texto: English translation by S. A. B. Mercer (1952), Sacred Texts

fuentes/ensenanza-de-ptahhotep/resumen.texto: Collection of maxims attributed to the vizier Ptahhotep, who is said to have served under King Isesi (5th Dynasty). The surviving manuscripts date from the Middle Kingdom; the dating of the composition is disputed.

fuentes/ensenanza-de-ptahhotep/por_que_i.texto: It is an early example of wisdom literature on conduct, authority and dealings with superiors and inferiors.

fuentes/ensenanza-de-ptahhotep/leer.0.ti.texto: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and Ke'Gemni, Project Gutenberg

fuentes/historia-de-sinuhe/resumen.texto: Tale of a courtier who flees Egypt after the death of Amenemhat I, lives among the Asiatics of the Levant and returns in old age to the pardon of King Senusret I.

fuentes/historia-de-sinuhe/por_que_impor.texto: A portrait of the Middle Kingdom and of the Egyptian view of the Asiatic world, and a masterpiece of the classical language.

fuentes/historia-de-sinuhe/leer.0.titulo.texto: Maspero, Popular Stories of Ancient Egypt (1915), Internet Archive

fuentes/textos-de-los-sarcofagos/resumen.texto: Funerary spells painted on coffins of the First Intermediate Period and the Middle Kingdom, partly inherited from the Pyramid Texts and now available to private individuals.

fuentes/textos-de-los-sarcofagos/por_que.texto: They document the democratization of the afterlife and are the forerunner of the Book of the Dead.

fuentes/papiro-westcar/resumen.texto: Collection of tales of magicians told to King Khufu, including the birth of the first three kings of the 5th Dynasty. The manuscript dates from the Hyksos period; its exact provenance is unknown.

fuentes/papiro-westcar/por_que_importa.texto: It shows how Middle Kingdom Egyptians imagined the court of the pyramid builders.

fuentes/papiro-westcar/leer.0.titulo.texto: Petrie, Egyptian Tales, First Series (1913), Internet Archive

fuentes/papiro-ebers/resumen.texto: The longest surviving Egyptian medical treatise: more than 700 formulas and remedies, descriptions of diseases and incantations. It was bought in Luxor by Georg Ebers in 1873.

fuentes/papiro-ebers/por_que_importa.texto: It informs us about the Egyptian pharmacopoeia and medical ideas and their mix of practice and magic.

fuentes/papiro-ebers/leer.0.titulo.texto: Ebers, Papyrus Ebers (1875 facsimile edition), Internet Archive

fuentes/papiro-edwin-smith/resumen.texto: Treatise on trauma surgery with 48 cases ordered from the head downward. It is a 17th-century BC copy of a probably older text.

fuentes/papiro-edwin-smith/por_que_impor.texto: It is the first medical text with an empirical method of diagnosis and prognosis.

fuentes/libro-de-los-muertos/soporte.texto: Papyri, mummy bandages and tomb walls

fuentes/libro-de-los-muertos/resumen.texto: Collection of spells (called by the Egyptians the Book of Coming Forth by Day) written on papyri and placed beside the dead, including chapter 125 on the judgment before Osiris.

fuentes/libro-de-los-muertos/por_que_imp.texto: It is the main source for Egyptian beliefs about the afterlife in the New Kingdom and later.

fuentes/libro-de-los-muertos/leer.0.titu.texto: Budge, The Book of the Dead, Project Gutenberg

fuentes/gran-himno-a-aton/soporte.texto: Inscription in the tomb of Ay at Amarna

fuentes/gran-himno-a-aton/resumen.texto: Hymn to the solar disk Aten, composed in the time of Akhenaten and preserved in the tomb of Ay. It celebrates the Aten as creator and sustainer of all peoples.

fuentes/gran-himno-a-aton/por_que_import.texto: It is the central expression of the Amarna religion, often compared with Psalm 104.

fuentes/gran-himno-a-aton/leer.0.titulo.texto: Great Hymn to the Aten, Wikisource

fuentes/cartas-de-amarna/resumen.texto: Some 380 tablets with the diplomatic correspondence of the pharaohs Amenhotep III and Akhenaten with the kings of Babylon, Mitanni and Hatti and the vassal rulers of the Levant.

fuentes/cartas-de-amarna/por_que_importa.texto: They show the system of international relations of the Late Bronze Age.

fuentes/cartas-de-amarna/leer.1.titulo.texto: The Tell el-Amarna texts, in “Egyptian Literature” (Wikisource)

fuentes/poema-de-pentaur/resumen.texto: Verse account of the Battle of Kadesh in year 5 of Ramesses II, carved at Karnak, Luxor, Abydos, the Ramesseum and Abu Simbel and copied on papyri. A papyrus attributes it to the scribe Pentaur.

fuentes/poema-de-pentaur/por_que_importa.texto: It is royal propaganda, but together with Hittite sources it allows the study of one of the greatest battles of Antiquity.

fuentes/poema-de-pentaur/leer.0.titulo.texto: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 3 (1906), Internet Archive

fuentes/tratado-egipcio-hitita/soporte.texto: Stela at Karnak and clay tablet at Hattusa

fuentes/tratado-egipcio-hitita/resumen.texto: Peace treaty between Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III in the former's year 21. Egyptian (at Karnak and the Ramesseum) and Hittite (in Akkadian) versions survive, with clauses on alliance and extradition.

fuentes/tratado-egipcio-hitita/por_que_i.texto: It is the oldest international treaty whose text survives in both versions.

fuentes/tratado-egipcio-hitita/leer.0.ti.texto: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 3 (1906), Internet Archive

fuentes/papiro-abbott/resumen.texto: Report of a commission inspecting the royal tombs of Thebes in the time of Ramesses IX. It belongs to the group of papyri from the tomb-robbery trials.

fuentes/papiro-abbott/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the crisis of security and authority at the end of the New Kingdom.

fuentes/papiro-abbott/leer.0.titulo.texto: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 4 (1906), Internet Archive

fuentes/papiros-de-elefantina/resumen.texto: Archive of contracts, letters and documents of the Jewish and Aramean garrison of Elephantine under Persian rule, including the petition to rebuild its temple of Yahweh.

fuentes/papiros-de-elefantina/por_que_im.texto: It is the main archive for daily life under the Persians and for the history of ancient Judaism outside Judea.

fuentes/papiros-de-elefantina/leer.0.tit.texto: Cowley, Aramaic Papyri of the Fifth Century B.C. (1923), Internet Archive

fuentes/piedra-de-rosetta/resumen.texto: Priestly decree of Memphis in honor of Ptolemy V, inscribed in three scripts. It was found in 1799 at Rosetta by French soldiers.

fuentes/piedra-de-rosetta/por_que_import.texto: The Greek version made it possible to decipher hieroglyphs in the 19th century.

fuentes/piedra-de-rosetta/leer.0.titulo.texto: Budge, The Rosetta Stone, Project Gutenberg

fuentes/papiros-de-oxirrinco/soporte.texto: Papyri found in the city's rubbish dumps

fuentes/papiros-de-oxirrinco/resumen.texto: Hundreds of thousands of fragments from the city of Oxyrhynchus, ranging from contracts and letters to literary and Christian texts. The first excavations were carried out by Grenfell and Hunt from 1896.

fuentes/papiros-de-oxirrinco/por_que_imp.texto: They offer the best picture of daily life in Greco-Roman and Byzantine Egypt.

fuentes/papiros-de-oxirrinco/leer.0.titu.texto: Grenfell and Hunt (eds.), The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Part I (1898), Internet Archive

fuentes/historias-de-herodoto-libros-ii-.texto: Histories, Books II and III (Euterpe and Thalia)

Book II describes Egypt, its geography, customs, religion and the history of its kings; Book III, the Persian conquest by Cambyses. Herodotus visited Egypt c. the mid-5th century BC and records what the priests told him.
It is the oldest and most famous Greek source on Egypt, with errors and valuable information.
Herodotus, Histories II, trans. A. D. Godley (Perseus)
Herodotus, Histories III, trans. A. D. Godley (Perseus)

fuentes/aegyptiaca-de-maneton/soporte.texto: Lost work, preserved in fragments quoted by Josephus, Africanus and Eusebius

fuentes/aegyptiaca-de-maneton/resumen.texto: History of Egypt in three books, written for the Ptolemaic king by an Egyptian priest. It was lost, but its division into 30 dynasties remains the basis of the chronology.

fuentes/aegyptiaca-de-maneton/por_que_im.texto: It gave us the division into dynasties, often disputed but indispensable.

fuentes/aegyptiaca-de-maneton/leer.0.tit.texto: Manetho, trans. W. G. Waddell (LacusCurtius, Loeb 1940)

fuentes/biblioteca-historica-diodoro-lib.texto: Book I of Diodorus deals with the mythological origins and history of Egypt, with descriptions of the Nile and the kings, taken from Hecataeus of Abdera and others.
It is one of the few extensive descriptions of Egypt from antiquity.

fuentes/geografia-de-estrabon-libro-xvii.texto: Book XVII describes Egypt and North Africa, including Alexandria, its harbors, the Museum and the cities of the Nile, partly based on the author's visit c. 25-20 BC.
It gives a picture of Egypt at the time of the Roman annexation.
Strabo, Geography XVII, trans. H. L. Jones (Perseus)

fuentes/sobre-isis-y-osiris/resumen.texto: Treatise by Plutarch on the myth of Isis and Osiris, with philosophical interpretations. It is the most complete account of the myth from antiquity.

fuentes/sobre-isis-y-osiris/por_que_impo.texto: It shows how an educated Greek of the 2nd century understood Egyptian religion.

fuentes/contra-apion/resumen.texto: Defense of Judaism written by Flavius Josephus. It quotes Manetho on the Hyksos and the Exodus, which makes it an indirect source for the Aegyptiaca.

fuentes/contra-apion/por_que_importa.texto: Much of what survives of Manetho comes from here.

fuentes/khitat-de-al-maqrizi/resumen.texto: Great topographical and historical description of Egypt and Cairo, with information on the cities, monuments, quarters, religions and Egyptian history since antiquity.

fuentes/khitat-de-al-maqrizi/por_que_imp.texto: It is the richest medieval source on Cairo and its past.

fuentes/khitat-de-al-maqrizi/leer.0.titu.texto: Al-Maqrizi, Khitat, ed. Wiet (IFAO, 1924), Internet Archive

fuentes/suluk-de-al-maqrizi/titulo.texto: Kitāb al-Sulūk (History of the Mamluk Sultans)

fuentes/suluk-de-al-maqrizi/resumen.texto: Chronicle of Egypt under the Ayyubids and Mamluks, from Saladin to the author's own time.

fuentes/suluk-de-al-maqrizi/por_que_impo.texto: Essential for the history of the sultans of Cairo.

fuentes/suluk-de-al-maqrizi/leer.0.titul.texto: Al-Maqrizi, Histoire des sultans mamlouks, trans. Quatremère (1837)

fuentes/relacion-de-egipto-abd-al-latif/.texto: Description of Egypt by the Baghdadi physician Abd al-Latif, who lived there in the late 12th century: the pyramids, daily life and the famine of 1200-1202.
An eyewitness to life in Egypt in Ayyubid times.
Abd al-Latif, Relation de l'Égypte, trans. S. de Sacy (1810)

fuentes/description-de-l-egypte/autor.texto: Commission of Sciences and Arts of Egypt

fuentes/description-de-l-egypte/resumen.texto: Monumental work by the scholars who accompanied Napoleon in Egypt, with plates of monuments, natural history and the modern state of the country.

fuentes/description-de-l-egypte/por_que_.texto: It founded Egyptology with its drawings of monuments that have since been altered.

fuentes/lettre-a-m-dacier/resumen.texto: Letter from Champollion to the secretary of the Academy announcing his method for reading royal names in hieroglyphs, the basis of the decipherment.

fuentes/lettre-a-m-dacier/leer.0.titulo.texto: Champollion, Lettre à M. Dacier (1822), Internet Archive

fuentes/precis-du-systeme-hieroglyphique.texto: First systematic exposition of the hieroglyphic writing system, with phonetic, ideographic and determinative signs.
It established that the script combined sounds and meanings.
Champollion, Précis du système hiéroglyphique (1824), Internet Archive

fuentes/ancient-records-of-egypt/resumen.texto: Five-volume edition of translations of Egyptian historical inscriptions, from the beginnings to the Persian conquest.

fuentes/ancient-records-of-egypt/por_que.texto: A classic compilation of historical documents, still widely cited.

fuentes/ancient-records-of-egypt/leer.0..texto: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 1 (1906), Internet Archive

fuentes/ancient-records-of-egypt/leer.1..texto: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 2 (1906), Internet Archive

fuentes/ancient-records-of-egypt/leer.2..texto: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 3 (1906), Internet Archive

fuentes/ancient-records-of-egypt/leer.3..texto: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. 4 (1906), Internet Archive

fuentes/a-history-of-egypt-breasted/titu.texto: A History of Egypt from the Earliest Times to the Persian Conquest

fuentes/a-history-of-egypt-breasted/resu.texto: Survey of the history of ancient Egypt by the founder of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago.

fuentes/a-history-of-egypt-breasted/por_.texto: It shows how the history of ancient Egypt was understood at the beginning of the 20th century.

fuentes/a-history-of-egypt-breasted/leer.texto: Breasted, A History of Egypt (1905), Internet Archive

fuentes/a-history-of-egypt-petrie/titulo.texto: A History of Egypt, vol. I (to the 16th Dynasty)

fuentes/a-history-of-egypt-petrie/resume.texto: First volume of Flinders Petrie's history of Egypt, based on his excavations and his method of seriation of finds.

fuentes/a-history-of-egypt-petrie/por_qu.texto: Work by the archaeologist who systematized excavation methods in Egypt.

fuentes/a-history-of-egypt-petrie/leer.0.texto: Petrie, A History of Egypt, vol. I (1894), Internet Archive

fuentes/egypt-of-the-pharaohs/resumen.texto: General introduction to the history of pharaonic Egypt by a great philologist.

fuentes/ancient-egypt-anatomy-of-a-civil.texto: Ancient Egypt: Anatomy of a Civilization
Study of Egyptian society through archaeology, economics and ideology, by a Cambridge archaeologist.
An anthropological approach to Egyptian history.

fuentes/oxford-history-of-ancient-egypt/.texto: The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt
Collective history of ancient Egypt edited by Ian Shaw, with chapters by specialists and the conventional chronology.
It is the usual reference for the chronology.

fuentes/ancient-egyptian-literature-lich.texto: Annotated anthology of Egyptian texts translated into English, in three volumes.
The standard translation of Egyptian literature.

personas/narmer/resumen.texto: King of the late Predynastic period, associated with the unification. He is usually identified with the Menes of the king lists, although the identification is debated.

personas/imhotep/resumen.texto: High official of Djoser (3rd Dynasty), traditionally the architect of the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. He was deified centuries later.

personas/ptahhotep/resumen.texto: Vizier of King Isesi (5th Dynasty), to whom a famous wisdom teaching is attributed. It is doubtful that he composed it.

personas/hatshepsut/resumen.texto: Queen of the 18th Dynasty who ruled as king from c. 1479 to 1458 BC, known for a famous expedition to Punt and her temple at Deir el-Bahari.

personas/tutmosis-iii/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty, he reigned nominally from c. 1479 and alone from 1458 BC; he led 17 campaigns in the Levant, among them Megiddo.

personas/akenaton/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty (c. 1353-1336 BC) who promoted the exclusive worship of the Aten and founded Akhetaten (Amarna).

personas/nefertiti/resumen.texto: Great Royal Wife of Akhenaten, with a prominent role in the cult of the Aten. Her ultimate fate is uncertain.

personas/ramses-ii/resumen.texto: Pharaoh of the 19th Dynasty who reigned for about 66 years (c. 1279-1213 BC). Protagonist of Kadesh and of the treaty with the Hittites.

personas/maneton/resumen.texto: Egyptian priest, from Heliopolis or Sebennytos, who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek under the early Ptolemies (3rd century BC).

personas/ptolomeo-i/resumen.texto: General of Alexander who took control of Egypt in 323 BC and founded the Ptolemaic dynasty; he proclaimed himself king in 305 BC. His birth dates are approximate.

personas/cleopatra-vii/resumen.texto: Last queen of the Ptolemaic dynasty. An ally of Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, she lost to Octavian and took her own life.

personas/hipatia/resumen.texto: Neoplatonist teacher in Alexandria, murdered by a Christian mob in 415. The sources give a date between 350 and 370 for her birth.

personas/diodoro-siculo/resumen.texto: Sicilian historian who, in the time of Caesar and Augustus, wrote a universal history in 40 books, with a visit to Egypt around 60 BC. His portrait of the Gauls (V.25-32) follows mainly Posidonius.

personas/estrabon/resumen.texto: Greek geographer from Amaseia, in Pontus; he visited Egypt with Aelius Gallus around 25-20 BC and wrote a Geography in 17 books. He was not in Gaul or Hispania: what he tells of the Celts (books III and IV) he takes mostly from Posidonius and Polybius.

personas/plutarco/resumen.texto: Greek writer from Chaeronea, author of the Parallel Lives and the Moralia, including On Isis and Osiris.

personas/champollion/resumen.texto: Frenchman who deciphered hieroglyphs in 1822 on the basis of the Rosetta Stone and other texts, and founded Egyptology.

personas/petrie/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, first professor of Egyptology at University College London; he introduced seriation dating.

personas/al-maqrizi/resumen.texto: Historian of Mamluk Cairo, author of chronicles and of a great topographical description of Egypt.

hechos/unificacion-de-egipto/resumen.texto: The first unified Egyptian state takes shape under the first kings, with Narmer-Menes as the traditional figure. Conventional date; the exact sequence of events is debated.

hechos/piramide-escalonada-de-saqqara/re.texto: The first large stone construction in Egypt is built, traditionally the work of the architect Imhotep for Djoser.

hechos/gran-piramide-de-giza/resumen.texto: Khufu (4th Dynasty) builds the largest of the Giza pyramids in about 20 years, according to the usual estimates.

hechos/reunificacion-de-mentuhotep-ii/ti.texto: Reunification of Egypt by Mentuhotep II

hechos/reunificacion-de-mentuhotep-ii/re.texto: Mentuhotep II of Thebes defeats the kings of Herakleopolis and reunifies the country, thus beginning the Middle Kingdom.

hechos/expulsion-de-los-hicsos/resumen.texto: Ahmose I takes Avaris, expels the Hyksos and reunifies Egypt, thus beginning the New Kingdom. Approximate date.

hechos/reinado-de-hatshepsut/resumen.texto: Hatshepsut rules as king; she builds her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari and sends an expedition to Punt.

hechos/batalla-de-meguido/resumen.texto: Thutmose III defeats a coalition of Canaanite cities in his first campaign and takes Megiddo after a siege.

hechos/reforma-de-amarna/resumen.texto: Akhenaten imposes the worship of the Aten and moves the capital to Akhetaten (Amarna). After his death the city is abandoned and the traditional cult is restored.

hechos/batalla-de-qadesh/resumen.texto: Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II clash by the Orontes in one of the largest chariot battles of antiquity. Both claimed victory.

hechos/tratado-egipcio-hitita-hecho/resu.texto: Ramesses II and Hattusili III sign a treaty of peace and alliance, drawn up in Egyptian and Hittite versions.

hechos/procesos-por-robo-de-tumbas/resum.texto: In the time of Ramesses IX, the looting of tombs in the Theban necropolis is investigated, and papyri record the proceedings.

hechos/conquista-persa-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Cambyses II defeats the pharaoh Psamtik III near Pelusium and Egypt becomes a satrapy of the Persian Empire.

hechos/conquista-de-alejandro/titulo.texto: Conquest of Egypt by Alexander the Great

hechos/conquista-de-alejandro/resumen.texto: Alexander enters Egypt without serious resistance, is accepted as pharaoh and visits the oasis of Siwa.

hechos/fundacion-de-alejandria/resumen.texto: Alexander founds on the coast of the Delta the city that will become the capital of the Ptolemies.

hechos/biblioteca-de-alejandria/resumen.texto: The early Ptolemies create the Museum and its great library, the center of learning of the Hellenistic world. The exact date is uncertain.

hechos/decreto-de-menfis-piedra-de-roset.texto: A synod of priests issues the decree in honor of Ptolemy V, later inscribed on the Rosetta Stone.

hechos/batalla-de-accio/resumen.texto: Octavian defeats the fleet of Mark Antony and Cleopatra off the coast of Greece.

hechos/anexion-romana-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Octavian takes Alexandria, Cleopatra takes her own life and Egypt becomes a Roman province, the personal property of the emperor.

hechos/muerte-de-hipatia/resumen.texto: Hypatia is murdered by a Christian mob, amid the tensions between the prefect Orestes and the patriarch Cyril.

hechos/conquista-arabe-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Amr ibn al-As conquers Egypt from the Byzantines, takes Babylon (the fortress) and Alexandria, and founds the camp of Fustat.

hechos/fundacion-de-el-cairo/resumen.texto: The Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli founds al-Qahira as the caliph's residence; the city becomes the capital.

hechos/expedicion-de-napoleon/resumen.texto: The French army lands at Alexandria with a commission of scholars; the occupation lasts until 1801. The expedition opens the modern era of Egyptology.

hechos/desciframiento-de-los-jeroglifico.texto: Champollion announces in the Lettre à M. Dacier the method for reading hieroglyphic writing, based on the Rosetta Stone.

hechos/tumba-de-tutankamon/titulo.texto: Discovery of the tomb of Tutankhamun

hechos/tumba-de-tutankamon/resumen.texto: Howard Carter, sponsored by Lord Carnarvon, discovers the almost intact tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62).

lugares/menfis/resumen.texto: Capital of the Old Kingdom and administrative center during much of Egyptian history; it declined with the rise of Alexandria and Fustat.

lugares/tebas/resumen.texto: Capital of the New Kingdom and city of Amun; today Luxor and Karnak, with the necropolises on the west bank.

lugares/abidos/resumen.texto: Necropolis of the first kings and center of the cult of Osiris.

lugares/amarna/resumen.texto: Akhetaten, the capital founded by Akhenaten and abandoned after his death; the site where the Amarna letters were found.

lugares/alejandria/resumen.texto: Founded by Alexander, Ptolemaic capital and great center of learning, with its Museum and its Library.

lugares/heliopolis/resumen.texto: Great center of the solar cult of Ra and its theology, northeast of present-day Cairo.

lugares/giza/resumen.texto: Necropolis of Memphis with the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure and the Great Sphinx.

lugares/saqqara/resumen.texto: Great necropolis of Memphis, with the Step Pyramid of Djoser and the Pyramid Texts.

lugares/elefantina/resumen.texto: Frontier island at the First Cataract, seat of a Jewish and Aramean garrison with its papyri.

lugares/oxirrinco/resumen.texto: Nome capital in Middle Egypt, famous for the discovery of thousands of papyri.

lugares/pi-ramses/resumen.texto: Delta capital of Ramesses II, today Qantir; seat of the court during the late New Kingdom.

lugares/fustat/resumen.texto: First Arab capital of Egypt, founded by Amr ibn al-As; today part of Cairo.

lugares/el-cairo/resumen.texto: Founded by the Fatimids; capital of the country and a great center of the Islamic world.

lugares/deir-el-medina/resumen.texto: Village of the workers on the tombs of the Valley of the Kings, with thousands of ostraca and papyri on daily life.

lugares/fayum/resumen.texto: Oasis city in the Faiyum, about 100 km southwest of Cairo. It was occupied from the Epipaleolithic and settled from the 5th millennium BC (Bagnall). At the latest in the Old Kingdom it was Shedet, the main center of the cult of the crocodile god Sobek, and the Greeks called it Crocodilopolis, after the sacred crocodile Petsuchos, adorned with gold and gems. Ptolemy II named the nome Arsinoite after his sister and wife Arsinoe II; the city was also called Ptolemais Euergetis and, in Roman times, Arsinoe (Arsinoe in Arcadia), and with Christianity it became an episcopal see suffragan to Oxyrhynchus. The modern name comes from the Coptic Phiom, “the sea” or “the lake,” after Lake Moeris.
